cues.text: Hi Linda. Can you spare a few minutes?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Hello Matthew, no problem.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: I just wanted to talk to you about temporary work placements ... I’ve never really thought there was a good reason for doing one. I’ve got some savings, so I don’t really need the money at the moment.
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: But I’ve had an email from the university about a vacancy that looks quite interesting. You did a placement last year didn’t you?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: I did, yes. In my case I wanted to find out if I was making the right career choice before I began applying for permanent jobs. I thought I wanted to work in car manufacturing but I wasn’t sure. So I applied to Toyota.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: What was the application process like?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Lengthy. There were a lot of different parts to it. The dullest one was a psychometric test - you know, when you have to answer loads of questions about yourself.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: And you’re trying to guess what’s the best thing to say!
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Yes. Then there was an activity that we did in groups, which I found really fascinating. Engineers are renowned for being a bit unsociable, but I thought we made a great team.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: And we had an individual task too. We had to sort through various business documents and prioritise them. It was just like what you have to do as a student really, just with different content.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: What exactly were you doing on the placement?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: I was helping to design some diagnostic software to identify any waste in the car assembly process
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: Do you mean waste of materials?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: No, time anything that can speed the process up helps to cut costs.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: How did the work placement compare to being a student? Was it hard work?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Yes, it was. I’d had full-time work before - I’ve done various unskilled jobs during university holidays, and some of those involved long hours - so I thought I’d find it easy. I was wrong though. I think when you’re on placement you’re always trying to prove yourself ...
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: So you push yourself hard to succeed?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Yes. But I got a lot of support from my employers. They were always helpful. And then at the end of the placement I was given formal feedback.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: Do you mean on your engineering ability?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Well, no, I didn’t really need that because we had team meetings every other day, and so I had the chance to discuss technical issues and ask about anything that wasn’t clear. The evaluation was about general workplace things, like organisational ability, initiative ... That sort of thing …
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: I get the impression you think you benefited from the placement ... ?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Well the best thing is that they’ve offered me a job for next year! Depending on my exam results of course, but still ...
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: A permanent one?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Yes! But apart from that I learned so much . The industrial environment was much more demanding than the academic one, so my general skills improved. Like time Management ... meeting deadlines ... And on the technical side I learned new software packages like MS Project.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: Well, I think you’ve convinced me that work placements are worthwhile ... But while you’re here can you give me advice on something else?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: I’m about to make a start on the Engineering Materials module, and I’ve got a booklist here - can you have a quick look and tell me what you would recommend - that’s if you can remember?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Let’s see ... I do remember some of them ... Yes, this one ...The Science of Materials. I found the subject quite hard generally, but this book is very accessible so it suited me. It doesn’t cover everything though …
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: What about this one then . Materials Engineering?
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Oh yes, I do remember that. But it’s a bit out-of-date now isn’t it, unless it’s a new edition?
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: I don’t think so ...
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: But what I liked about it were the pictures. They really helped to understand the descriptions. It’s useful just from that point of view ... Let’s see ... What else? Oh yes ... That one there - Engineering Basics - I think out of all these that’s got the widest coverage ...
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: But I’ve looked at the contents page, and it hardly mentions nanotechnology.
cues.speaker: Matthew

cues.text: Yes, you’re right. The Evolution of Materials does though. It’s a recent publication so it covers all the latest developments. It’s a bit thin on the nineteen sixties though, and that decade was quite important.
cues.speaker: Linda

cues.text: Well it sounds as if they all complement each other in some ways. I don’t suppose you can lend me .
cues.speaker: Matthew
